title: The placebo problem
text: Give patients an inert pill, tell them honestly that it contains nothing active, and something curious can still happen: they improve. This is the placebo effect, medicine's most inconvenient curiosity, and it is so {{1}} (PERSIST) that every careful drug trial must control for it. New treatments are measured against dummy pills precisely because feeling better is not the same as being better, and {{2}} (PERCEIVE) improvement can mask the absence of genuine progress. The effect grows stronger when the treatment looks {{3}} (IMPRESS): injections outperform tablets, branded packaging outperforms plain wrappers, and a doctor in a white coat outperforms them all. Surprisingly, deception is not required. In one trial, patients who knew their pills were dummies still reported {{4}} (MEANING) relief, presumably because the ritual of treatment itself carries weight. Researchers explain much of the phenomenon through {{5}} (EXPECT): the brain anticipates recovery and quietly delivers part of it. Rather than a bystander in its own healing, the mind turns out to be an active {{6}} (PARTICIPATE). Some physicians now prescribe placebos openly, and the {{7}} (HONEST) appears to cost nothing — a result that would once have seemed frankly {{8}} (BELIEF).

gaps.explanation: 'perceived improvement' — improvement as it appears, from perceive.
'looks impressive' — the treatment causes the impression.
'an active participant' — the person form of participate.
'the honesty appears to cost nothing' — noun from honest.
'seemed frankly unbelievable' — negative prefix un- on the adjective.
